title: Black Sea Attacks Threaten Global Wheat Supply
summary:
The Black Sea has become the most dangerous it has been since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022. Since mid-July, attacks on commercial ships have increased sharply, and both sides are striking vessels to hurt the other's economy.

According to Ambrey, a British maritime risk firm, there were more than 210 strikes on commercial vessels between July and the end of September. It attributed 125 to Ukraine and 88 to Russia. Ukraine has targeted ships connected to Moscow's "shadow fleet" and Russian port infrastructure; Russia has hit Ukrainian ports and ships. The danger is real for sailors. Mykola Lupar, a 29-year-old navy commander, patrols from the port of Chornomorsk and says he can usually count his time on open water in minutes before rushing back to shore. "It's very dangerous," he said. "For the merchant fleet, I would say there's almost no chance to stay safe in our waters."

Together, Russia and Ukraine supply roughly a quarter of the world's wheat exports. Analysts estimate their combined exports are down 60 percent from last year. That has already pushed global wheat prices higher and raised concerns about food shortages, especially in nearby regions.

"It's not only a Ukrainian problem. This is a problem for the whole region," said Dmytro Barinov, president of the Ukrainian Ports Association. He said people will feel food shortages by October or November.

Russia's Defence Ministry insists it only targets military assets. After striking a cargo vessel in Chornomorsk on Thursday, officials accused the ship of supplying the military. Barinov rejects that, saying Russia is hitting civilian ships. He pointed to a July missile strike on the Golden Leo near Odesa that killed ten people; Ukrainian officials said it was carrying corn. Barinov compared the attacks to hunting, since merchant ships are slow and have no military defences. "It's like hunting for an elephant from a helicopter," he said.

Ukraine has also struck Russian ships and ports. In August, a Ukrainian missile and drone strike hit the port of Novorossiysk, damaging two major grain export terminals. Turkey has tried to secure a limited truce, but those efforts have failed so far. Back in 2022, the UN and Turkey secured the Black Sea Grain Initiative to keep ships moving to Ukrainian ports, but it fell apart after a year when Russia refused to renew it.
why_it_matters: Black Sea grain feeds much of the world, so when this shipping lane turns into a war zone the first people to suffer are families in poorer countries who already spend a large share of their income on bread and cooking oil.

background_read: The Black Sea (a sea bordered by Ukraine, Russia, Turkey and several other countries) has long been one of the world's most important routes for grain, and the region is often called the 'breadbasket of Europe'.

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, global wheat prices jumped sharply, and countries in North Africa and the Middle East that depend on imported wheat felt the squeeze hardest.

In July 2022 the United Nations (a group where almost every country meets to discuss world problems) and Turkey (a country that sits between Europe and Asia and controls the straits leading into the Black Sea) brokered the Black Sea Grain Initiative, which allowed grain ships to leave Ukrainian ports safely.

Russia pulled out of that deal in 2023, and shipping in the region has been far riskier ever since. Turkey keeps trying to revive at least a limited agreement, because the Black Sea is on its doorstep and grain prices affect its own economy.

perspectives.description: Russia's Defence Ministry insists it only strikes military assets and says the cargo vessel hit at Chornomorsk was supplying Ukraine's army. From this view, hitting ports and shadow-fleet ships is a way to weaken an enemy's war economy rather than an attack on ordinary traders.

Ukrainian officials and port leaders such as Dmytro Barinov argue the strikes are hitting civilian ships that have no defences at all, and that sailors and wheat-importing countries pay the price. They point to the July missile strike on the Golden Leo near Odesa, which killed ten people, as proof the targets are civilian.

Researchers note that the danger runs both ways: Ambrey attributes more strikes to Ukraine than to Russia, and Ukraine has damaged grain terminals at Novorossiysk. Historically, attacks on shipping rarely stop because one side decides to be nicer — they end when a third party, like Turkey or the UN in 2022, offers both sides something in exchange for safe passage.

The immediate question is whether Turkey can revive even a limited truce, and whether insurance companies will keep covering ships that sail into these waters. If they stop, exports stay low and wheat prices stay high, which would be felt most in North African and Middle Eastern countries that rely on Black Sea grain.
